hero.headline: DeSantis signs $117.6 billion Florida budget with $1.6 billion in vetoes
hero.body:
Gov. Ron DeSantis signed Florida's next state budget Monday in Tampa, putting his final approval on a spending plan that takes effect July 1. The budget totals $117.6 billion after DeSantis used his veto power to cut approximately $1.6 billion through rerouted funds and about $800 million in line-item vetoes. DeSantis presented the budget as a continuation of fiscal discipline, noting it marks the fourth consecutive year Florida has reduced its overall state budget. "Who else is doing that?" the governor said at the signing ceremony.

The budget allocates $30 billion for K-12 education, a significant increase from the less than $22 billion spent when DeSantis took office. Teacher salaries receive $1.56 billion in funding, with $200 million specifically directed toward educators with at least 10 years of experience. The state's transportation budget reaches nearly $16 billion and will fund road projects across multiple regions, including Tampa Bay, Central Florida, South Florida, Southwest Florida, Northeast Florida and the Panhandle. State workers in several categories will also see pay increases, including correctional officers, state law enforcement officers, firefighters and park rangers.

DeSantis highlighted Florida's strong financial position, noting the state expects to end the next fiscal year with approximately $18 billion in reserves, maintains a fully funded rainy-day fund and holds an AAA credit rating from major rating agencies. He also emphasized that Florida has retired more than half of its taxpayer-supported debt during his tenure. Environmental initiatives received substantial funding, with more than $9 billion directed toward Everglades restoration and water quality improvements, plus more than $2 billion for the Resilient Florida program to help communities prepare for storms and flooding.

The signing ceremony at Hillsborough College carried political significance given the campus's connection to a proposed Tampa Bay Rays stadium district. Lawmakers included $50 million for campus improvements as part of the broader redevelopment effort. DeSantis said the college would benefit significantly if the stadium proposal moves forward. However, the budget signing was not without controversy. DeSantis had previously warned that local projects backed by lawmakers who did not support his priorities could face vulnerability to vetoes, a statement that drew criticism from Democrats and others who questioned whether the veto pen was being used as political leverage. The governor's office has not yet released a complete list of all budget vetoes.

cards.headline: Woman, 78, killed after SUV rolls backward in Port St. Lucie driveway
cards.teaser: A 78-year-old woman died Sunday morning after a 2016 Lincoln MKX SUV rolled backward and struck her in a residential driveway in Port St. Lucie.
cards.body:
A 78-year-old woman was killed Sunday morning after an SUV rolled backward and struck her in a residential driveway in Port St. Lucie, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. The incident happened at approximately 10:47 a.m. when a 2016 Lincoln MKX SUV that was parked in the driveway began rolling backward. The woman was standing outside the vehicle near the open driver's door when the door struck her, knocking her to the ground. Her adult son, 59, was in the passenger seat and had started the vehicle. The cause of the rollback remains under investigation.

The woman was rushed to Lawnwood Hospital in Fort Pierce, where she was pronounced deceased at 11:19 a.m. Neighbors who knew the woman for several years spoke about her acts of kindness. "I saw the ambulance, the fire trucks, and two or three police cars. I felt sad, sad because I've known her for many years," said neighbor Daisy Cardona. "On Sundays, they would bring us bread, cupcakes, donuts, and sometimes cakes that were this big. May she rest in peace and my condolences to her family." This is an ongoing investigation.

cards.headline: Supreme Court rules states can count ballots arriving after Election Day
cards.teaser: The Supreme Court rejected a Republican-led challenge to laws in more than half the states that permit mailed ballots to arrive and be counted days after the election if postmarked by Election Day.
cards.body:
The Supreme Court on Monday ruled that states can count ballots that arrive after Election Day, rejecting a Republican-led attack on laws in more than half the states and the District of Columbia that permit mailed ballots to arrive and be counted some number of days after the election, provided they are postmarked by Election Day. The decision spares officials the headache of changing their ballot rules just a few months before the 2026 midterm congressional elections. In just over half those states, the more forgiving deadlines apply only to ballots cast by military and overseas voters.

The legal challenge was part of President Donald Trump's broader attack on most mail balloting, which he has said breeds fraud despite strong evidence to the contrary and years of experience in numerous states. The court heard arguments in March in a case from Mississippi pitting the state against Trump's Republican administration and the Republican and Libertarian parties. At issue was whether federal law sets a single Election Day that requires ballots to be both cast by voters and received by state officials. The federal appeals court in New Orleans had struck down a Mississippi law allowing ballots to be counted if they arrive within five business days of the election and are postmarked by Election Day.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office identifies Fort Pierce diver found dead near inlet
cards.teaser: Greer Boyd, 63, of Fort Pierce died Friday while attempting to recover a trolling motor that had fallen overboard from a fishing boat near the Fort Pierce Inlet.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office has identified the diver found dead Friday near the Fort Pierce Inlet as Greer Boyd, 63, of Fort Pierce. According to investigators, Boyd was fishing with friends earlier in the day when the boat's trolling motor became detached and went overboard. The group returned to the area with diving equipment to attempt recovery of the motor. Boyd entered the water alone, and only his buoyancy compensator and air tank were located approximately 40 yards from the boat.

Coast Guard Station Fort Pierce received a Mayday call over VHF Channel 16 at approximately 11:30 a.m. Friday regarding the missing diver. Following the distress call, the Coast Guard notified the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, which immediately deployed four vessels to assist in the search. Martin County Fire Rescue Lt. Daniel DeGrazia, who was off-duty at the time, assisted in the response. DeGrazia recovered Boyd's body at the bottom of the ocean in approximately 55 feet of water. An autopsy is scheduled today.

cards.headline: Supreme Court rejects Trump appeal in E. Jean Carroll sexual abuse case
cards.teaser: The Supreme Court declined to overturn a jury's finding that President Trump sexually abused writer E. Jean Carroll and later defamed her, leaving a $5 million verdict in place.
cards.body:
The Supreme Court on Monday rejected President Donald Trump's appeal to overturn a jury's finding that he sexually abused writer E. Jean Carroll at a Manhattan department store in the mid-1990s and later defamed her. The high court declined to take up the case in a brief, unexplained order. Trump's lawyers had argued that the $5 million verdict was based on "highly inflammatory" evidentiary rulings, including testimony from two other women who accused Trump of sexual abuse decades ago. Trump has denied all three women's allegations. His attorneys contended the judge broke federal evidence rules and framed the case as a distraction from Trump's duties as president, though the verdict came before his return to the White House. Attorney Justin D. Smith, who wrote in court documents that "this mistreatment of a President cannot be allowed to stand," has since been nominated by Trump to be an appeals court judge.

Carroll, a longtime advice columnist and former TV talk show host, testified at a 2023 trial that Trump turned a friendly spring 1996 encounter into a violent attack in a dressing room at Bergdorf Goodman, a luxury retailer across the street from Trump Tower. The jury found Trump liable for defaming Carroll when he denied her allegation in 2022. A second jury awarded Carroll an additional $83.3 million after a defamation trial. Trump is appealing that ruling, though it is not yet before the Supreme Court.

cards.headline: 400-pound black bear killed by car on Martin County highway
cards.teaser: A male black bear was struck and killed Monday morning on Southwest Martin Highway near Southwest Warfield Boulevard after running into the roadway.
cards.body:
A 400-pound male black bear was killed Monday morning after being struck by a car on Southwest Martin Highway near Southwest Warfield Boulevard, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The motorist immediately stopped and called authorities following the collision. Deputies responding to the scene learned from the driver that the bear ran into the roadway before being struck by the vehicle. The driver was not injured, but the bear died at the scene. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission removed the bear from the roadway, and traffic is now flowing normally through the area.

The Martin County Sheriff's Office said the collision serves as a reminder of the wildlife present along rural Martin County roadways, particularly during early morning and evening hours when animals are most active. This marks the second bear sighting on the Treasure Coast this month. A black bear was previously caught on camera swimming through a waterway in the Town Park community of Port St. Lucie.

cards.headline: Jupiter Fire Rescue deploys 2 firefighters to Venezuela earthquake relief
cards.teaser: Two Jupiter Fire Rescue firefighters deployed to Venezuela as part of a FEMA Urban Search and Rescue Task Force with less than 24 hours notice.
cards.body:
First responders from Jupiter, Delray Beach, and Palm Beach County fire departments have deployed to Venezuela as part of a FEMA Urban Search and Rescue Task Force to assist with relief efforts. Jupiter Fire Rescue says its 2 firefighters are among a group of 80 deployed to the region. The crew was sent with less than 24 hours notice and is expected to remain in Venezuela for at least two weeks.

The mission focuses on search and rescue operations in collapsed structures, ranging from large buildings to smaller homes. The team brought heavy-duty equipment for breaking, cutting, breaching, and stabilization, as well as technical rope rescue tools. Stephen Shaw, deputy fire chief of operations for Jupiter Fire Rescue, said the deployment reflects the department's commitment to helping those in need. Shaw said the experience will also strengthen the department when the crew returns home, noting that the learning and skills being practiced will benefit the department as it continues to grow.

cards.headline: Alligator Alcatraz detainees scattered across U.S. as legal battles continue after facility closure
cards.teaser: After the controversial Everglades detention facility shut down, detainees have been sent to facilities across the country, creating challenges for families and immigration attorneys.
cards.body:
Immigration attorney Richard Hujber said detainees from the closed Alligator Alcatraz facility have been scattered to detention centers in Louisiana, Texas, New Mexico, and as far as Tacoma, Washington. Hujber explained that transferring detainees to facilities across different circuit courts creates significant legal challenges, as immigration law varies by region. With bond now out of reach for some detainees, many face difficult decisions about whether to continue pursuing residency or asylum or to self-deport instead. Gov. Ron DeSantis reported that approximately 21,000 people were deported from the facility since it opened nearly a year ago.

For some families, the facility's closure brought relief. Anna Maria Hernandez's cousin was released just before Alligator Alcatraz shut down and is now under an order of supervision, allowing him to drive, work and live in the U.S. However, Hujber emphasized that the fight ahead remains difficult and ultimately depends on the detainees themselves. The Baker County facility in North Florida continues to operate, leaving many former Alligator Alcatraz detainees and their families facing an uncertain future.

hero.headline: Vero Beach MusicWorks Launches Fourteenth Concert Season to Expand Cultural Tourism
hero.body:
Vero Beach's MusicWorks has launched its fourteenth concert season, positioning the city alongside cultural destinations including California, Texas, New York, Tennessee, Georgia, Illinois, Nevada, Arizona, Michigan and Massachusetts. The concert series aims to expand cultural tourism and inspire multi-state travel across participating regions.

The announcement marks a significant expansion for the Vero Beach cultural institution. MusicWorks continues to draw visitors from across the country, contributing to local tourism and economic activity in Indian River County.

Florida's alignment with these major cultural markets reflects the growing recognition of Vero Beach as a destination for performing arts. The concert series has become a fixture in the city's cultural landscape over its thirteen previous seasons.

The fourteenth season programming will continue MusicWorks' tradition of bringing professional concert performances to Vero Beach audiences. The organization's reach now extends to multiple states as it works to attract travelers interested in cultural experiences.

cards.headline: Boca Raton July 4 Market to Feature Kids Parade, Police and Fire Department Appearances
cards.teaser: The SoFlo Market will transform Boca Raton City Hall into a patriotic celebration on July 4 with a kids parade, live DJ, local vendors and the first 20 children receiving free gifts.
cards.body:
The SoFlo Market will transform Boca Raton City Hall into a patriotic celebration on Saturday, July 4, drawing families and shopping enthusiasts from across Palm Beach County. Founder and organizer Tatiana Freitas told WPTV the free monthly event will feature extra patriotic flair for Independence Day, including a kids' parade and DJ. The first 20 children through the gate will receive a free gift. Family entertainment options include face painting, a foggy bubble station, mini golf, balloon twisting, handmade crafts and desserts. The market's flamingo mascot will make a live appearance.

Local partnerships strengthen the celebration, with Boca Raton firefighters and police officers invited to share the day with residents. Kyle, Freitas' son, and Eddie, her husband, are part of the organizing team. The event runs from 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. at 201 West Palmetto Park Road with free admission and on-site generator power. Freitas said the market's mission is to uplift small local businesses and bring the community together, with the Independence Day edition always standing out among monthly events.

cards.headline: George Snow Scholarship Fund Awards Record $7.5 Million to 470 Students in Palm Beach and Broward Counties
cards.teaser: The Boca Raton nonprofit has distributed more than $45 million to over 4,100 students since its founding 40 years ago, making it the largest scholarship provider in Palm Beach County.
cards.body:
The George Snow Scholarship Fund, headquartered in Boca Raton, awarded more than $7.5 million in scholarships and support services to 470 students across Palm Beach and Broward counties in 2026, according to President Tim Snow. Founded over 40 years ago, the nonprofit has distributed more than $45 million to over 4,100 students, making it the largest scholarship provider in Palm Beach County. The program offers four-year commitments to ensure stability throughout college and bridges the gap between traditional financial aid and what students and families can afford.

Services extend beyond financial assistance to include mentorship, professional development, and resources like the College Compass podcast, according to Vice President of Development Jay Brandt. The fund operates the Doyle-Whelchel Scholars Boutique, led by Scholar Services Coordinator Garvey Antoine, which provides professional, formal, and casual wear for scholars preparing for interviews, internships, and campus life. One 2026 recipient, Zya Chow, a Wellington Community High School graduate, earned both the Royal Palm Hearing Aid Scholarship and the Davidowitz Family Caregiving Youth Scholarship and plans to attend Georgetown University.

cards.headline: New Florida law requires study before expanding Broward's Mount Trashmore landfill
cards.teaser: Gov. DeSantis signed legislation creating new procedural requirements before Broward County can approve any expansion of the Monarch Hill Landfill known as Mount Trashmore.
cards.body:
Broward won't be able to expand its semi-iconic trash heap as easily as it has in the past under legislation Gov. Ron DeSantis recently approved. DeSantis has signed HB 4039, which creates new procedural requirements before the county can approve any expansion of the Monarch Hill Landfill, known colloquially as Mount Trashmore. Under the new law, Broward must first commission an independent feasibility study evaluating environmental, public health, groundwater, traffic, odor, noise and cumulative impacts, while analyzing alternatives such as waste-to-energy technology. At least one public hearing, complete with a presentation of the study's findings, must be held within five miles of the landfill, with 30 days' public notice and with direct notice given to nearby property owners. No zoning change, permit, development order or other approval for an expansion may advance until both the study and hearing have been completed and publicly disclosed.

The measure came in response to Broward's highly contentious February 2025 vote to expand the Monarch Hill Landfill, despite fierce opposition from residents of Coconut Creek and Deerfield Beach. Broward Commissioners approved plans after months of deferrals, allowing the landfill to expand 24 acres horizontally and 100 feet vertically, roughly doubling its footprint. Coral Springs Democratic Rep. Dan Daley filed and carried the bill to passage without a Senate companion. After the Commission voted 5-3 in favor, with Vice Mayor Mark Bogen and Commissioners Lamar Fisher and Alexandra Davis voting no, Daley filed HB 4039. The bill passed unanimously in both chambers of the Legislature and is effective October.

Jean Carroll at a Manhattan department store in the mid-1990s and later defamed her. The high court declined to take up the case in a brief, unexplained order. Trump's lawyers had argued that the $5 million verdict was based on "highly inflammatory" evidentiary rulings, including testimony from two other women who accused Trump of sexual abuse decades ago. Trump has denied all three women's allegations. His attorneys contended the judge broke federal evidence rules and framed the case as a distraction from Trump's duties as president, though the verdict came before his return to the White House. Attorney Justin D. Smith, who wrote in court documents that "this mistreatment of a President cannot be allowed to stand," has since been nominated by Trump to be an appeals court judge.

Carroll, a longtime advice columnist and former TV talk show host, testified at a 2023 trial that Trump turned a friendly spring 1996 encounter into a violent attack in a dressing room at Bergdorf Goodman, a luxury retailer across the street from Trump Tower. The jury found Trump liable for defaming Carroll when he denied her allegation in 2022. A second jury awarded Carroll an additional $83.3 million after a defamation trial. Trump is appealing that ruling, though it is not yet before the Supreme Court.

cards.headline: St. Petersburg Mayor expected to select Gas Plant District developer after July 4
cards.teaser: Mayor Ken Welch will soon announce his selection for the developer or developers who will help shape the future of the nearly 100-acre Historic Gas Plant District in downtown St. Petersburg.
cards.body:
After months of evaluating proposals and gathering public feedback, St. Petersburg Mayor Ken Welch will soon select the developer or developers who will shape the future of the Historic Gas Plant District. According to Samantha Bequer, a spokesperson for the City of St. Petersburg, Welch is expected to announce his selection shortly after the Fourth of July holiday. The nearly 100-acre Historic Gas Plant District encompasses roughly 15% of downtown St. Petersburg, making it one of the city's largest redevelopment opportunities. Long before it became the site of Tropicana Field, the district was one of St. Petersburg's oldest African American neighborhoods established in the late 19th century. The neighborhood was permanently altered by the construction of Interstate 175, which displaced residents and divided the community. Hundreds more families and businesses were relocated in the 1980s when the city cleared the site for what became Tropicana Field.

When the city reopened the redevelopment process this year, Mayor Welch said the effort reflects his administration's broader JHOP initiative, which stands for Jobs, Housing, Economic Opportunity and Honoring the Promises. The selection will not conclude the redevelopment process. After Welch announces his decision, the proposal will move to the Community Benefits Advisory Council for review before city staff negotiates a term sheet and development agreement. Any final agreement will require City Council approval. Bequer said the city is targeting final approvals and a groundbreaking around the Summer of 2027 if the process stays on schedule.

cards.headline: Bogey Creek Preserve in Jacksonville expands by 4 acres
cards.teaser: The North Florida Land Trust brokered a conservation deal that adds 4 acres to the Bogey Creek Preserve in northern Duval County, bringing the total conservation area to 89 acres.
cards.body:
The Bogey Creek Preserve in northern Duval County is expanding by 4 acres following a conservation deal brokered by the North Florida Land Trust. The preserve, located about 10 miles north of downtown Jacksonville, previously contained more than 80 acres of protected land. NFLT officials purchased the additional property from Spencer Engineering and Exploration Co., whose owners are related to the original landowners who sold most of the existing preserve to the NFLT in 2006. Beaches Go Green, an environmental conservation group in Duval County's coastal area, contributed $60,000 to the acquisition. The total conservation area now stands at 89 acres.

The preserve entrance is located at 5500 Cedar Point Road in the vast wetland areas of North Jacksonville and is already open to the public. Trails are available from sunrise to sunset at the maritime hammock, and the property is part of a larger NFLT network covering about a mile of cypress swamps with picnic areas and kayak landings. It also connects to the Seven Creeks Recreation Area, a network of city, state and national park access. NFLT President and CEO Allison DeFoor said the organization is considering adding an outdoor learning center and will seek community input on the project. The expansion represents the smallest acreage among several substantial land acquisition deals the NFLT has completed this year.

hero.headline: 400-pound black bear struck and killed on Martin County highway Monday morning
hero.body:
A 400-pound male black bear died Monday morning after being struck by a vehicle on Southwest Martin Highway near Southwest Warfield Boulevard. The Martin County Sheriff's Office responded to the collision after the driver immediately stopped and reported the incident to authorities.

According to the driver's account to deputies, the bear suddenly ran onto the roadway and was hit by the car. The driver escaped injury in the crash, but the bear was killed at the scene. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission arrived afterward to remove the animal. Road conditions returned to normal shortly after the incident.

The collision underscores the importance of being alert to wildlife that inhabits rural Martin County roads. The sheriff's office noted that animals are particularly active during early morning and evening hours, when drivers should exercise extra caution. The incident marks the second bear encounter on the Treasure Coast within the past month. Earlier in June, a black bear was recorded on camera swimming through a waterway in the Town Park community of Port St. Lucie.

These sightings reflect the ongoing presence of black bears in the region and the need for both drivers and residents to remain vigilant. While fatal wildlife collisions on roadways are serious events, they serve as reminders about coexisting with Florida's animal populations in areas where human development meets natural habitats.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce diver identified after drowning near Fort Pierce Inlet while recovering boat motor
cards.teaser: Greer Boyd, 63, of Fort Pierce died Friday while diving alone to recover a trolling motor that fell off his boat near the Fort Pierce Inlet.
cards.body:
The St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office identified the diver found dead Friday near the Fort Pierce Inlet as Greer Boyd, 63, of Fort Pierce. Investigators said Boyd was fishing with friends earlier in the day when the boat's trolling motor became detached and went overboard. The group returned to the area with diving equipment to attempt recovery of the motor. Boyd entered the water alone, and only his buoyancy compensator and air tank were located approximately 40 yards from the boat.

Coast Guard Station Fort Pierce received a Mayday call over VHF Channel 16 at approximately 11:30 a.m. Friday regarding a missing diver. Following the distress call, the Coast Guard notified the Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, which immediately deployed four vessels to assist in the search. Martin County Fire Rescue Lt. Daniel DeGrazia, who was off-duty at the time, assisted in the operation. DeGrazia recovered the body of the missing diver at the bottom of the ocean in approximately 55 feet of water. An autopsy was scheduled.

hero.body:
The crash resulted in a three-mile backup on Interstate 95 northbound in St. Lucie County as emergency responders worked to clear the scene. Traffic delays affected motorists traveling through the area while crews addressed the incident.

The Florida Highway Patrol responded to the crash and managed traffic control during the emergency response. Other emergency personnel assisted at the scene to ensure the safety of both responders and motorists in the affected corridor.

The incident caused significant congestion on the northbound lanes of I-95. Drivers were advised to use alternate routes or expect delays while the roadway was being cleared and investigated.

Additional information regarding the cause of the crash and any injuries involved has not yet been released by authorities. The investigation remained ongoing at the time of the initial report.

cards.headline: Woman, 78, dies after SUV rolls backward in Port St. Lucie driveway
cards.teaser: A 78-year-old woman was killed Sunday morning when an SUV rolled backward and struck her in a residential driveway in Port St. Lucie.
cards.body:
A 78-year-old woman died Sunday morning after a 2016 Lincoln MKX SUV rolled backward and struck her in a residential driveway in Port St. Lucie. The incident occurred at approximately 10:47 a.m. The woman was standing outside the vehicle near the open driver's door when the SUV began rolling backward. The open door struck her, knocking her to the ground. Her adult son, 59, was in the passenger seat and had started the vehicle. The cause of the rollback remains under investigation by the Florida Highway Patrol.

The woman was transported to Lawnwood Hospital in Fort Pierce, where she was pronounced deceased at 11:19 a.m. Neighbors who knew the woman for several years shared memories of her kindness. "I saw the ambulance, the fire trucks, and two or three police cars. I felt sad, sad because I've known her for many years," said neighbor Daisy Cardona. "On Sundays, they would bring us bread, cupcakes, donuts, and sometimes cakes that were this big. May she rest in peace and my condolences to her family.

hero.body:

Living shorelines use natural materials and native vegetation to reduce erosion while maintaining habitat for marine life. The installation at Sebastian Inlet State Park represents an alternative to traditional hardened structures like seawalls.

The project is currently underway at the popular state park, which serves both Indian River and Brevard counties. Sebastian Inlet State Park attracts thousands of visitors annually for fishing, surfing, and beach recreation.
